power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_exact.title: Exact P-Values
stat_p_exact.summary_text: We found 1 imprecise *p* value out of 2 detected *p* values.

table.expanded: The model had excellent fit (χ2 = 10.0, DF = 11, p = 0.529, CFI = 1.000, TLI = 1.006, RMSEA = 0.000 [90% CI: 0.000; 0.052]).

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < 0.05", Text = "All estimates were statistically significant (p < 0.05)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.title: Non-Significant P Value Check
stat_p_nonsig.summary_text: We found 1 non-significant p value that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

table.expanded: The model had excellent fit (χ2 = 10.0, DF = 11, p = 0.529, CFI = 1.000, TLI = 1.006, RMSEA = 0.000 [90% CI: 0.000; 0.052]).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = 0.529", Sentence = "The model had excellent fit (χ2 = 10.0, DF = 11, p = 0.529, CFI = 1.000, TLI = 1.006, RMSEA = 0.000 [90% CI: 0.000; 0.052])."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

report: Below, we describe some best coding practices and give the results of automatic evaluation of these practices in the code files below. This check may miss things or produce false positives if your scripts are less typical.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list("File Name" = "Violence_Script.R", "% Comments" = "57%", "Missing Files" = 0L, "Absolute Paths" = 0L, "Code Between Libraries" = 1L), row.names = 1L, class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ```
#### Code Comments
Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code). All your code files had comments.
#### Missing Files
All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.
#### Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., './files') instead of absolute file paths (e.g., 'C://Lakens/project_dir/files') as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.
#### Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid `setwd()` in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author's own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No `setwd()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid `install.packages()` in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an `renv.lock`/`DESCRIPTION` for R, a `requirements.txt` for Python). No `install.packages()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Libraries / Imports
Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.
#### Packages / Dependencies
The code files load 3 distinct packages/libraries: lavaan, MASS, metafor. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).
#### Reproducible Environment

No `renv.lock` file, `sessionInfo()`/`session_info()` record, or `groundhog`/`checkpoint` date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an `renv.lock` (via the `renv` package), a `sessionInfo()` text dump, or a `groundhog`/`checkpoint` date-pin alongside the code.
#### Parsable code
All R-type code files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd) could be read in. There were no parsing issues.

text.text: Based on positive cross-lagged effects in data (N = 357, 51.5% female) from two waves of measurement, Swingler et al. concluded that violence exposure in early adolescence represents a prospective risk factor for conduct problems.
text.formatted: Based on positive cross-lagged effects in data (N = 357, 51.5% female) from two waves of measurement, <ref type="bibr">Swingler et al.</ref> concluded that violence exposure in early adolescence represents a prospective risk factor for conduct problems.

text.text: However, it is well known that cross-lagged effects may be spurious.

We fitted alternative models to data simulated to resemble the data used by Swingler et al. and found discrepant increasing, decreasing, and null effects of violence exposure on subsequent change in conduct problems depending on the analyzed model.
text.formatted: We fitted alternative models to data simulated to resemble the data used by <ref type="bibr">Swingler et al. and</ref> found discrepant increasing, decreasing, and null effects of violence exposure on subsequent change in conduct problems depending on the analyzed model.

text.text: A meta-analytic pooling of these discrepant effects did not differ significantly from zero.
Hence, the findings by Swingler et al. may have been spurious and their conclusion premature.

It is important for researchers to bear in mind that associations, including cross-lagged regression effects, in observational (i.e., nonexperimental) data may be spurious in order not to overinterpret findings.
We recommend researchers to scrutinize cross-lagged effects by fitting alternative models to data and to base conclusions on a juxtaposition of findings.
Keywords: analytic rigor; conduct problems; crosslagged panel models (CLPM); juxtaposition of findings; violence exposure
The cross-lagged panel model (CLPM)
In cross-lagged panel models (CLPM), subsequent scores on two (or more) variables are regressed on initial scores on the same variables.
An effect of X1 on Y2 when adjusting for Y1 is often assumed, at least among researchers in psychology, to allow stronger conclusions compared with crosssectional and cross-lagged correlations.

For example, Swingler et al. (2026) reported statistically significant cross-lagged effects of initial violence exposure on subsequent conduct problems when adjusting for initial conduct problems among South African adolescents and concluded that violence exposure in early adolescence represents a prospective risk factor for conduct problems.

(2026)</ref> reported statistically significant cross-lagged effects of initial violence exposure on subsequent conduct problems when adjusting for initial conduct problems among South African adolescents and concluded that violence exposure in early adolescence represents a prospective risk factor for conduct problems.

text.text: However, it is well known that adjusted crosslagged effects may be spurious (e.g. Campbell and Kenny, 1999; Sorjonen et al., 2019).

The SPAM does not include direct effects between the longitudinal scores, meaning that such effects in statistical analyses, e.g., the CLPM, would be spurious.

The SPAM had good fit (Fig 2), indicating that the data analyzed by Swingler et al., and simulated and reanalyzed by us, may have been generated without direct effects between longitudinal scores on violence exposure and conduct problems.
text.formatted: The SPAM had good fit (Fig <ref type="figure">2</ref>), indicating that the data analyzed by <ref type="bibr">Swingler et al., and simulated</ref> and reanalyzed by us, may have been generated without direct effects between longitudinal scores on violence exposure and conduct problems.

text.text: The objective of this commentary was to scrutinize wingler et al.'s findings and conclusions of a prospective increasing effect of violence exposure on conduct problems.

When fitting alternative models to data, we found contradictory increasing, decreasing, and null effects of violence exposure on subsequent change in conduct problems and a meta-analytic pooling of these discrepant effects did not differ significantly from zero.

Moreover, the spurious prospective associations model (SPAM) had excellent fit, suggesting that the data analyzed by Swingler et al., and simulated and reanalyzed by us, may have been generated without direct effects between longitudinal scores on violence exposure and conduct problems.
text.formatted: Moreover, the spurious prospective associations model (SPAM) had excellent fit, suggesting that the data analyzed by <ref type="bibr">Swingler et al., and simulated</ref> and reanalyzed by us, may have been generated without direct effects between longitudinal scores on violence exposure and conduct problems.

text.text: Taken together, our reanalyses indicate that the findings by Swingler et al. may have been spurious and their conclusions premature.

It is important for researchers to bear in mind that associations in observational (i.e., nonexperimental) data, including adjusted cross-lagged regression effects, may be spurious in order not to overinterpret findings.

For increased analytic rigor, we recommend researchers to scrutinize crosslagged effects by fitting, as we did here, alternative models to data and to base conclusions on a juxtaposition of the findings.
